title: Redwood cost econ discovery w/ Auriga Capital
summary: Discovery focused on per-token pricing, batching/caching levers, and whether Hosted, Dedicated, or Private makes sense given Auriga's budgets and latency needs. Redwood AE+SE walked through cost model, batching impact, caching, dedicated reserved capacity, and pilot structure. Next steps: pricing sheet, benchmark plan, security docs, pilot scoping.
topics: dedicated vs hosted vs private economics
transcript:
[00:00] Ethan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Ethan from Redwood. Uh, Chloe mentioned you guys were doing a deep dive on cost today?
[00:12] Maya (CTO): Yeah thanks, Ethan. We want to understand, like, basically cost per inference, how batching and caching change that, and whether we should go hosted or reserved.
[00:25] Samir (SE): Great, we'll run through the per-token model and then some knobs — batching, prefix/KV caching, quantization profiles, and dedicated capacity commit math.
[00:35] Liam (Head of Data): Quick context: our production workload is about 120M tokens/day now for internal tooling, with spikes to 250M during end-of-quarter. Latency SLO is 300-400ms for the interactive flows, longer is ok for async. Budget: we're trying to cap to ~ $20k/month for the initial pilot.
[00:58] Jordan (Quant): Oh okay that's helpful — also want to note that 80% of our queries are short, like 30-60 tokens, but we have long generations for reports ~800-1k tokens.
[01:15] Ethan: Right, so per-token price varies by model and whether it's hosted or dedicated. For hosted we have a simple per-token rate — e.g., base model M1 at $0.0009/1k input + $0.0016/1k output (example), but you get the benefit of no reserved infra.
[01:35] Maya: Wait, those units confuse us a bit. Can you put that in cents per token?
[01:40] Samir: Sure, rough math: that means ~0.0000025 - 0.000003 per token, depends on direction. But the important part is effective cost which depends on how much batching & caching we can do.
[01:56] Liam: How big is the win from batching? We have a lot of concurrent small requests.
[02:03] Samir: Good question. For small requests, continuous batching can aggregate many small prompts onto a GPU and amortize the kernel cost. In practice we see 10-30% cost improvements for interactive traffic with small batch sizes, up to 2-3x improvements for very batch-friendly workloads (like offline scoring). But it increases median latency modestly — 50-150ms extra depending on queueing policy.
[02:30] Jordan: So for our 300-400ms SLO, is that safe?
[02:33] Samir: For most of our customers yes, you can configure max latency budget and target percentiles; Redwood's runtime will cap batching to keep p95 under your bound. For dedicated clusters you can also provision headroom so batching doesn't push you over.
[02:48] Maya: What about prefix/KV caching? Our quant workflows have lots of repeated contexts for the same models.
[02:54] Ethan: That's where you get big wins — prefix caching (we call it KV cache) can reduce repeated token work. If you have repeated prefixes across requests (e.g., identical system prompts or shared document context), effective per-token cost drops because the KV cache avoids recomputing earlier layers. Depending on repeat rate, you can see 20-60% savings on token compute.
[03:18] Liam: Are those caches global or per-VM? We have multi-region users.
[03:22] Samir: They can be configured per-deployment and we support multi-region cache sync for dedicated/private deployments; hosted has region-local caching with configurable TTLs. There's also a smart prefix hashing so cache hits are efficient.
[03:36] Jordan: Any caveat with privacy/regulatory — cached contexts stored in memory?
[03:40] Ethan: By default caches are ephemeral in memory and not persisted; for Private you can option to control retention and encryption. We'll share the security doc but short answer: caches are not logged to disk by default and you can disable persistence.
[03:55] Sofia (Procurement): From procurement, do you have reserved pricing for committed spend?
[03:59] Ethan: Yes — Redwood Dedicated has reserved capacity with discounted per-token-equivalent pricing because you're buying GPU-hours. We can structure a monthly commit; typical discounts 20-40% depending on term and size. For Private/on-prem we do enterprise licensing plus support.
[04:18] Maya: Can you walk through a sample commit math? For our pilot $20k/month, what does that buy?
[04:24] Samir: Sure — quick back-of-envelope. If your effective tokens/day is 120M -> ~3.6B tokens/month. At hosted per-token raw rates that could be ~ $11k-18k depending on model mix. But that's raw, not considering batching & caching. If we assume 30% effective reduction via caching/batching, that drops to ~ $8k-12k. With a dedicated 1-2 GPU pool reserved for baseline throughput, you pay a fixed VM/GPU monthly plus much lower marginal token costs — that can stabilize pricing and help with spikes.
[04:58] Liam: The numbers seem promising. How do you handle spikes to 250M/day?
[05:03] Samir: We offer burst capacity options on Dedicated that let you go above reserved baseline for short periods, billed at a higher marginal rate. Also routing policies let us route non-critical workloads to cheaper regions or model variants.
[05:16] Jordan: Model variants? You mean quantized versions?
[05:19] Samir: Exactly. We support multiple variants: FP16, int8, 4-bit quant — each has different latency/cost/quality tradeoffs. For many quant workloads int8 or 4-bit gives 2-4x throughput improvements with minimal quality loss for standard LLM tasks. We'll help you run evals to validate.
[05:37] Maya: Ok, quality regressions worry our quants. We need a way to measure.
[05:41] Ethan: We always recommend a small eval set and baseline runs; Redwood Optimize will suggest quant profiles and report regressions tied to prompt sets. We'll include that in the benchmark plan.
[05:52] Maya: Great. What about data egress and network costs, especially if we go Private vs Hosted?
[05:58] Samir: For hosted, standard cloud egress applies if you're cross-region; we try to keep inference, model, and clients in same region. For Private, it's inside your network so no Redwood egress. Dedicated has options to colocate in customer VPC to avoid egress. We'll share the deployment topology doc.
[06:15] Liam: Can you share an example pricing sheet?
[06:18] Ethan: Yep — we have a shared pricing spreadsheet and a sample cost model. I'll drop the link: shared:redwood-pricing-pilot.xlsx and public doc https://redwood.ai/docs/pricing (note: example numbers).
[06:30] Sofia: Procurement notes: we need line items for committed monthly cost, overage, pilot terms, and cancellation SLA.
[06:36] Ethan: Understood, we'll provide a clean line-item quote after we agree on pilot scope.
[06:41] [07:00] Jordan: Slightly naive question: per-token pricing — do you charge for both input + output tokens?
[07:05] Samir: Yes typically both; some customers negotiate an output-only model for specific flows but standard is input + output.
[07:12] Maya: For our workflows majority of cost is output tokens since our responses are long.
[07:16] Ethan: Then batching is less effective on output-dominated workloads, but caching still helps if prefixes repeat.
[07:24] Liam: What about latency targets with quantized models on shared hosted?
[07:29] Samir: Quantized models often have lower per-token latency but could be limited by GPU memory and batching logic. On hosted we offer model-specific performance profiles — the Redwood catalog shows p50/p95 for each model variant under typical batch sizes. If you need strict p95 targets, Dedicated is safer.
[07:47] Maya: Could you give an example: say you want p95 < 400ms on 1k token generations — what's realistic?
[07:55] Samir: For 1k tokens, 400ms is aggressive; you'd likely want a dedicated GPU with optimized kernels and small batch size; we could hit 400ms p50 easily, p95 depends on queueing and tokenization — we should run a bench.
[08:12] Ethan: That's one reason the pilot matters. We do a small benchmark with your actual prompts and measure cost/latency across variants.
[08:20] Jordan: How long does a standard pilot take?
[08:23] Ethan: Usually 2-4 weeks for initial bench + one week for integration. If we do a deeper POC (routing and scale) maybe 4-8 weeks.
[08:33] Sofia: On legal stuff, we need SOC2 and data residency info.
[08:36] Ethan: We'll send the security pack (SOC 2, ISO docs, SAML/SSO details). For Private we can meet residency and KMS/HSM requirements.
[08:47] Maya: Back to numbers — can you show sensitivity to caching hit rate?
[08:51] Samir: Sure. If you have a 40% cache hit rate and typical cost per token of $0.000003, effective compute reduces by 40% for those requests — mathematically cost = base_cost * (1 - hit_rate) + cache_overhead. So 40% hit -> ~40% savings on compute tokens. Then batching multiplies on top.
[09:10] Liam: What's cache memory footprint per session?
[09:13] Samir: Depends on sequence length; typical short sessions very small. For large contexts we recommend a dedicated cache node sizing plan; we'll include memory estimates in the benchmark write-up.
[09:24] [10:00] Jordan: Are there any hidden costs, like licensing on certain models?
[10:05] Ethan: We mainly serve open and Redwood-curated models; some third-party commercial models might have licensing fees — we'll call them out. Also training/fine-tuning is separate.
[10:16] Maya: Can you show a scenario: hosted for pilot then move to dedicated after 3 months? Are migrations smooth?
[10:22] Samir: Yes we support migration paths — same API/credentials, you can pin model versions, and we can do a staged cutover with canaries. Rollouts and traffic splitting are supported in Console.
[10:34] Liam: Do you have tooling to show token-level cost breakdowns by route?
[10:38] Ethan: Yes Redwood Console shows token-level cost, model, route breakdowns and tracing to attribute expensive calls. This is really useful to identify optimization targets.
[10:48] Jordan: About model quantization — you mentioned 4-bit. Are quality regressions likely for our quant work?
[10:53] Samir: It depends; many customers find 4-bit to be fine for classification and many generation tasks but quant-sensitive tasks like longform summarization sometimes need int8 or FP16. We'll run your test prompts.
[11:06] Maya: Ok, let's talk contractual constraints: we might need data isolation and encryption at rest, plus audit logs.
[11:12] Ethan: For Dedicated and Private we provide VPC options, KMS integration, and audit logs with export. Hosted has audit logs too but the Private plane gives you more control.
[11:22] Sofia: Any minimums for Dedicated?
[11:25] Ethan: Typically a 3-6 month commit for Dedicated; minimum depends on GPU pool size. We'll propose options for a pilot-friendly small reserved pool with month-to-month flexibility.
[11:36] [12:00] Liam: How do you price token costs on Dedicated? Is it still per-token or some hybrid?
[12:06] Samir: It's hybrid — you pay a fixed monthly for reserved GPU hours + lower marginal compute token equivalent. For modeling we convert GPU-hours into an effective token capacity to compare apples-to-apples.
[12:18] Jordan: If we overrun the pool how are overages charged?
[12:22] Ethan: Overages during bursts billed at a higher per-minute or per-token-equivalent rate, configurable in the contract. We can also set hard caps to protect budgets.
[12:32] Maya: For our 250M/day spikes, can Dedicated handle it?
[12:36] Samir: Sure with appropriate headroom or burst configuration, or hybrid approach: baseline on Dedicated + cloud-hosted burst. That keeps baseline costs predictable and handles peaks.
[12:48] Maya: We're sensitive to long-tail costs. Any tooling to forecast spend?
[12:52] Ethan: Console has forecast models and we provide spreadsheets. We'll run a 90-day projection in the pilot.
[13:00] [14:00] Jordan: A couple more technical Qs: are KV cache hits deterministic across quant variants?
[14:05] Samir: Mostly yes; caching is at the token embedding/KV layer so variants that change tokenization might change hits. We'll account for that in evals.
[14:16] Liam: Do you support custom batching windows per route?
[14:20] Samir: Yes per-route batching policies, latency caps, priority queues.
[14:25] Maya: Ok sounds good. Let's summarize next steps.
[14:30] Ethan: Quick recap: we'll send pricing spreadsheet, a proposed pilot scope (2-4 weeks bench + 1 week integration), security pack, and a benchmark plan to run your representative prompts across hosted/dedicated/quant variants. We'll also include a sample cost model showing sensitivity to cache hit rate and batching.
[14:50] Sofia: Procurement: include a line for a pilot PO and cancellation terms.
[15:00] Maya: We'll schedule the bench next week if you can provide the onboarding doc and small guide.
[15:05] Ethan: Absolutely. Any final questions?
[15:10] Jordan: One last — can we get a cost per 1M effective tokens after 30% caching and 15% batching? Just back-of-envelope.
[15:18] Samir: If base is $12 per 1M tokens, 30% caching -> 8.4 per 1M, then 15% batching -> ~7.14 per 1M effective tokens. We'll put exact sensitives in the spreadsheet.
[15:34] Maya: Nice. Thanks everyone.
[15:36] Ethan: Thank you — we'll send the artifacts and book the kickoff.
[15:40] [END]
